Background Acute kidney injury (AKI) is increasingly encountered in community settings and contributes to morbidity, mortality, and increased resource utilization worldwide. In low-resource settings, lack of awareness of and limited access to diagnostic and therapeutic interventions likely influence patient management. We evaluated the feasibility of the use of point-of-care (POC) serum creatinine and urine dipstick testing with an education and training program to optimize the identification and management of AKI in the community in 3 low-resource countries. Methods and findings Patients presenting to healthcare centers (HCCs) from 1 October 2016 to 29 September 2017 in the cities Cochabamba, Bolivia; Dharan, Nepal; and Blantyre, Malawi, were assessed utilizing a symptom-based risk score to identify patients at moderate to high AKI risk. POC testing for serum creatinine and urine dipstick at enrollment were utilized to classify these patients as having chronic kidney disease (CKD), acute kidney disease (AKD), or no kidney disease (NKD). Patients were followed for a maximum of 6 months with repeat POC testing. AKI development was assessed at 7 days, kidney recovery at 1 month, and progression to CKD and mortality at 3 and 6 months. Following an observation phase to establish baseline data, care providers and physicians in the HCCs were trained with a standardized protocol utilizing POC tests to evaluate and manage patients, guided by physicians in referral hospitals connected via mobile digital technology. We evaluated 3,577 patients, and 2,101 were enrolled: 978 in the observation phase and 1,123 in the intervention phase. Due to the high number of patients attending the centers daily, it was not feasible to screen all patients to assess the actual incidence of AKI. Of enrolled patients, 1,825/2,101 (87%) were adults, 1,117/2,101 (53%) were females, 399/2,101 (19%) were from Bolivia, 813/2,101 (39%) were from Malawi, and 889/2,101 (42%) were from Nepal. The age of enrolled patients ranged from 1 month to 96 years, with a mean of 43 years (SD 21) and a median of 43 years (IQR 27–62). Hypertension was the most common comorbidity (418/2,101; 20%). At enrollment, 197/2,101 (9.4%) had CKD, and 1,199/2,101 (57%) had AKD. AKI developed in 30% within 7 days. By 1 month, 268/978 (27%) patients in the observation phase and 203/1,123 (18%) in the intervention phase were lost to follow-up. In the intervention phase, more patients received fluids (observation 714/978 [73%] versus intervention 874/1,123 [78%]; 95% CI 0.63, 0.94; p = 0.012), hospitalization was reduced (observation 578/978 [59%] versus intervention 548/1,123 [49%]; 95% CI 0.55, 0.79; p < 0.001), and admitted patients with severe AKI did not show a significantly lower mortality during follow-up (observation 27/135 [20%] versus intervention 21/178 [11.8%]; 95% CI 0.98, 3.52; p = 0.057). Of 504 patients with kidney function assessed during the 6-month follow-up, de novo CKD arose in 79/484 (16.3%), with no difference between the observation and intervention phase (95% CI 0.91, 2.47; p = 0.101). Overall mortality was 273/2,101 (13%) and was highest in those who had CKD (24/106; 23%), followed by those with AKD (128/760; 17%), AKI (85/628; 14%), and NKD (36/607; 6%). The main limitation of our study was the inability to determine the actual incidence of kidney dysfunction in the health centers as it was not feasible to screen all the patients due to the high numbers seen daily. Conclusions This multicenter, non-randomized feasibility study in low-resource settings demonstrates that it is feasible to implement a comprehensive program utilizing POC testing and protocol-based management to improve the recognition and management of AKI and AKD in high-risk patients in primary care. Etienne Macedo and colleagues report on a point-of-care testing program for acute kidney injury and disease in high-risk primary care patients. Author summary Why was this study done? The study was designed to assess the feasibility of implementing interventions to optimize care of acute kidney injury (AKI). We used a comprehensive 5R approach—risk, recognition, response, renal support, and rehabilitation—to test the intervention in resource-constrained regions in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. What did the researchers do and find? Patients seen in community healthcare centers were screened and assigned a risk level for AKI based on their presenting signs and symptoms. Patients with moderate to high risk were approached for consent and enrolled in the study, underwent kidney function assessment, and were followed for their disposition and outcomes. Kidney function was assessed using point-of-care (POC) tests that included a test strip for measuring creatinine level in the blood using a portable device and a urine dipstick test to evaluate for proteinuria. What do these findings mean? The ISN 0by25 trial successfully demonstrated the utility of a symptom-based health assessment risk score coupled with a POC creatinine and urine dipstick test in early recognition of kidney disease and appropriate triaging and management of patients presenting to primary healthcare centers in low-income countries. Kidney dysfunction was associated with an increased risk of mortality, which was higher in patients with a moderate severity of AKI. Recognition and management of patients was facilitated by the combination of the POC test and guidance through teleconsultation. extracted_data.document_summary: This multi-country feasibility study, part of the ISN 0by25 trial, investigated the implementation of a comprehensive program for recognizing and managing community-acquired acute kidney injury (AKI) and acute kidney disease (AKD) in low-resource settings (Bolivia, Nepal, Malawi). The program combined point-of-care (POC) serum creatinine and urine dipstick testing with an education and training program for healthcare providers and teleconsultations with referral hospital physicians. The study demonstrated the feasibility of this approach in improving early identification and management of kidney disease in high-risk primary care patients, leading to reduced hospitalization rates and influencing management, despite high baseline rates of kidney dysfunction and mortality. The intervention facilitated the identification of more AKI patients, including more severe cases, compared to an observation phase.

treatment_details.therapy_type: A comprehensive intervention program combining healthcare provider education and training, point-of-care (POC) serum creatinine and urine dipstick testing, mobile digital technology-enabled teleconsultations, and fluid therapy for the recognition and management of Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) and Acute Kidney Disease (AKD).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The program was structured in a 4-month observation phase, a 2-month training phase, and a 6-month intervention phase. Healthcare providers and physicians in community health centers received training on AKI risk assessment, recognition, POC test use (serum creatinine and urine dipstick), interpretation, and management protocols, including the STOP AKI protocol, with real-time guidance via teleconsultation from referral hospital physicians. POC testing for serum creatinine was performed at enrollment and re-measured at 7 days, 1, 3, and 6 months follow-up, along with urine dipstick tests for proteinuria. During the intervention phase, patients received more fluids (both oral and intravenous; 75% received fluid therapy) compared to the observation phase, leading to reduced hospitalization (59% vs 49%, p<0.001). No specific quantitative doses for fluids or detailed dose-response comparisons for the educational intervention or testing frequency were reported, as the study focused on feasibility.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Used diagnostically for AKI definition: increase by >=26.5 µmol/l within 48 hours, or increase to >1.5 times baseline within 7 days. For AKI recovery: complete (returned to or below enrollment value) or partial (lower than peak but higher than enrollment). At 1 month, serum creatinine was lower than at enrollment in 84% (336/402) of AKI patients (no history of CKD) and 85.5% (241/282) of AKD patients. Over 66% of patients had kidney abnormalities based on initial POC test, and over 40% of AKI patients showed a decline, suggesting resolving AKI.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Waste product of muscle metabolism; a key indicator of glomerular filtration rate, kidney function, and potential damage or recovery.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Diagnosis, risk assessment, recognition, management, and monitoring of community-acquired Acute Kidney Injury (AKI), Acute Kidney Disease (AKD), and Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) in primary healthcare settings within low-resource countries (Bolivia, Nepal, Malawi), including assessment of recovery and progression.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A primary diagnostic marker for AKI, AKD, and CKD, indicating impaired kidney function, damage, or recovery. Elevated levels predict higher risk for AKI, CKD progression, hospitalization, and mortality. Declining levels can indicate resolving AKI or kidney impairment of unknown chronicity (AKD).

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Detected via urine dipstick; used diagnostically as a criterion for kidney damage (<3 months) in AKD definition. Found in 192 patients and in combination with reduced eGFR in 218 patients. More than half of patients had proteinuria and/or decreased eGFR at enrollment.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicates damage to the kidney's filtration barrier, allowing protein leakage into urine, signifying kidney dysfunction or disease, particularly glomerular or tubular injury.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Diagnosis, risk assessment, and screening for Acute Kidney Injury (AKI), Acute Kidney Disease (AKD), and general kidney damage in primary healthcare settings within low-resource countries.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A key indicator of kidney damage or dysfunction, used in conjunction with creatinine and eGFR to diagnose AKI, AKD, or CKD, and assess disease severity and risk.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Defined as <60 ml/min/1.73 m2 for CKD and AKD. Reduced in 789 patients overall; more than half of patients had decreased eGFR at enrollment. 7.8% (20/258) of NKD patients at 7 days had eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2 at 1 month. Used to define new-onset CKD and CKD progression (decreased from enrollment value).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Measures the rate at which kidneys filter blood, indicating overall kidney filtration capacity and health.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Diagnosis and classification of Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) and Acute Kidney Disease (AKD), monitoring kidney function, and detecting new-onset CKD and progression during follow-up in patients at risk for AKI.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: A primary indicator of kidney function, crucial for diagnosing and staging CKD and AKD (value <60 ml/min/1.73 m2), and assessing overall kidney health. Reduced eGFR indicates impaired kidney function and increased risk for AKI/CKD.
